text: If they had signed that treaty, we would not be arguing about it now.
If the archive had been destroyed, historians would still be repeating the old story.
If I did not read three papers a day, I would have missed it entirely.
If he were a more cautious man, he would never have made that call.
My students always want the story to have a hero. And it does, more or less. What they do not like is that it also has a broken satellite and a man who was not supposed to be on duty.
So if the other officer had been there, we might be having a very different conversation now.
That is the honest answer, and it makes people uncomfortable. Procedure said report it. He waited. Everything hung in the balance for about four minutes.
Was it judgement or was it a fluke? Because those are very different lessons to draw.
Both, and he said so himself. He thought five missiles were too few for a real attack. That reasoning was sound. That he happened to be the one in the chair was not.
It is easy to second-guess him now. If I were in that chair with four minutes, I am not sure I would have waited.
Nobody is. And if he had reported it, the system above him would probably have paused too. Probably. That word is doing an enormous amount of work.
Which is why the story keeps being told. If it had a clean answer, it would have stopped being interesting years ago.
If they had signed it, we would not be arguing about it now.
The whole thing was contingent on one man being in that chair.
It is easy to second-guess a decision taken in four minutes.
Against all odds, the crisis was allowed to run its course.
Whether it was down to judgement or to luck is still argued about.

Just after midnight, the screen in front of him reported a launch. Then a second. In the end, five. Now, the system was new, it had cost an enormous amount of money, and it was saying, in effect, that a war had started. His instructions were not ambiguous. Report it upwards, immediately. And he had, at the outside, four minutes. What he did instead was think about the number. Five missiles. If you were opening a war of that kind, you would not send five. You would send hundreds. And so he decided, on that reasoning alone, that the system was wrong, and he waited. It was wrong. The satellite had misread sunlight on high cloud. The world found out about all of this ten years later, by accident, from a memoir.

I am going to argue against my own colleagues for a moment. The trouble with counterfactual history is not that it is frivolous. It is that it cannot be tested. Whatever you propose, I can propose the opposite with exactly the same confidence, and the argument is then decided by whoever tells the better story, which is not a standard of evidence. That said, I do not think it is worthless. Done carefully, it does one thing extremely well: it reminds you that the outcome you are studying was contingent, and that the people living through it did not know how it ended. So here is my rule, and I offer it seriously. Change one thing. Only one. And change it as late as possible, because the further back you go, the more you are simply writing fiction.
